9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

The incidence rate ratio is a marginal, population-average estimator: events per total person-time of exposure in the vaccinated cohort versus unvaccinated.

For an all-or-nothing mechanism the biology is a mixture. A fraction p is rendered completely non-susceptible, per-exposure hazard 0, and a fraction 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated with per-exposure hazard λ0. The marginal hazard that the incidence density actually estimates is the average over that mixture

h_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0,
h_U = λ0

so

IRR = h_V / h_U = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

constant in time and independent of follow-up. That p is the population-average reduction in risk per unit exposure time, i.e. per exposure opportunity, the proportion of exposures rendered non-infectious because the recipient belongs to the protected sub-cohort.

The h_v(t)=λ(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}] and the time-averaged IRR(T)<1-p that the A derivations quote is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected at time t, i.e. the hazard in the still-at-risk risk set after the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort has been progressively depleted by infection while the p completely protected fraction continues to accrue event-free person-time. That monotonic decline is a selection/depletion artefact of conditioning on survival, not the marginal incidence rate that an IRR is defined to estimate.

Protected individuals are still having exposure opportunities; they simply have zero events on that time. Counting their zero-event person-time in the denominator is exactly how a population-average rate is defined. It is not denominator inflation, it is the correct exposure time with zero risk. Removing it would condition on susceptibility and change the estimand to a within-susceptible conditional hazard, which is not the per-exposure efficacy the rate ratio is designed to capture.

On the marginal scale the cumulative risk ratio is also constant for all-or-nothing:
S_V(t)=p+(1-p)S_U(t) → F_V(t)=(1-p)F_U(t) → RR(t)=1-p , so 1-RR=p=1-IRR.
Both cumulative and rate scales recover the same susceptibility efficacy p.

If per-exposure vaccine efficacy is taken in its usual epidemiologic sense as the average reduction in infection probability per exposure opportunity at the cohort level, the 1-incidence rate ratio estimates it without systematic bias for an all-or-nothing vaccine. The apparent time dependence belongs to the conditional-on-survival hazard among survivors, not to the marginal rate used in practice.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The disagreement here is really about what “per-exposure” means in the incidence density, and I think the C camp has the marginal definition right.

An all-or-nothing vaccine is a mixture: a fraction p is rendered completely non-susceptible, hazard 0 per exposure, and a fraction 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated with per-exposure hazard λ0. An incidence density is events per total person-time, i.e. per total exposure opportunity. On that population scale the expected hazard in the vaccinated arm is the mixture

h_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p)λ0

and h_U = λ0. Hence the marginal rate ratio that a cohort IRR targets is

IRR = h_V / h_U = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

constant in time and independent of follow-up length. That p is the average reduction in risk per unit exposure time experienced by the vaccinated cohort: the proportion of exposure opportunities that are rendered non-infectious because the recipient belongs to the protected sub-cohort.

The time-declining expression

h_v(t)= λ(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}]

that is repeatedly quoted for the overestimate claim is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected at time t, i.e. the hazard in the still-at-risk risk set. It falls because the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort is progressively depleted by infection while the p never-at-risk fraction continues to accrue event-free person-time. That is a selection/depletion artefact of conditioning on survival, not the marginal incidence rate that an IRR estimates.

Counting person-time contributed by the permanently immune with zero events is not denominator inflation. Protected subjects are still having exposure opportunities; they simply have zero events on that time. Their zero-risk person-time is exactly how a population average rate expresses a reduction in risk per exposure. Removing it would condition on susceptibility and change the estimand to the hazard among residual susceptibles, which is not the per-exposure efficacy the rate ratio is designed for.

On the same mixture

S_V(t)=p+(1-p)S_U(t) ⇒ F_V(t)=(1-p)F_U(t) ⇒ RR(t)=1-p

so 1-RR = p = 1-IRR on the population average scale. The apparent time dependence of the A derivations is the conditional-on-survival hazard among survivors, and the fact that their time-averaged IRR(T)→0 as T→∞ is the tell: the vaccine does not become perfect with longer follow-up. The marginal, population-average reduction per exposure opportunity is p, and the incidence rate ratio recovers that susceptibility efficacy without systematic bias.

h_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0,
h_U = λ0

so

IRR = h_V / h_U = 1-p,    1-IRR = p

constant in time and independent of follow-up length. A susceptible vaccinee continues to have per-exposure risk λ0; the conditional hazard is falling because the composition of the still-uninfected group changes.

On the standard marginal definition the cumulative risk ratio agrees:

S_V(t)=p+(1-p)S_U(t)  ⇒  F_V(t)=(1-p)F_U(t)  ⇒  RR(t)=1-p,

The disagreement here is really about what we mean by per-exposure vaccine efficacy and what an incidence rate ratio is estimating in practice.

On the epidemiologic scale a rate is events per total person-time, i.e. the marginal population average hazard over the whole vaccinated cohort. For an all-or-nothing vaccine that population is a mixture: a fraction p has per-exposure hazard 0 and a fraction 1-p has the unvaccinated per-exposure hazard λ0. The marginal hazard that the incidence density actually estimates is therefore

h_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0
h_U = λ0

so that

IRR = h_V / h_U = 1-p   and   1-IRR = p

constant in time and independent of follow-up length. That p is the population-average reduction in risk per unit time, per exposure opportunity: the proportion of exposures rendered non-infectious because the recipient belongs to the protected sub-cohort. Protected individuals are still accumulating exposure opportunities, they simply have zero events on that time. Counting their zero-event person-time in the denominator is how a population average rate is defined; it is not denominator inflation, it is the correct marginal average.

The time-decreasing expression

h_v(t)= λ(1-p) e^{-λt} / [p+(1-p) e^{-λt}]

and the derived IRR(T) <1-p are the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected at time t, i.e. the hazard in the still-at-risk set after the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort has been selectively depleted by infection while the p completely protected fraction continues to accrue event-free person-time. That decline is a selection/depletion artefact of conditioning on survival, not the marginal incidence rate that an IRR is built from.

On the marginal scale the cumulative risk ratio is the same quantity: S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_u(t) ⇒ F_v(t)=(1-p)F_u(t) ⇒ RR(t)=1-p, so 1-RR=p=1-IRR. Both scales recover the susceptibility efficacy p for an all-or-nothing mechanism.

The disagreement here is really about what “per-exposure” means in the incidence density, and I think the C camp has the marginal definition right.

An all-or-nothing vaccine is a mixture: a fraction p is rendered completely non-susceptible, hazard 0 per exposure, and a fraction 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated with per-exposure hazard λ0. An incidence density is events per total person-time, i.e. per total exposure opportunity. On that population scale the expected hazard in the vaccinated arm is the mixture

h_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p)λ0

and h_U = λ0. Hence the marginal rate ratio that a cohort IRR targets is

IRR = h_V / h_U = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

constant in time and independent of follow-up length. That p is the average reduction in risk per unit exposure time experienced by the vaccinated cohort: the proportion of exposure opportunities that are rendered non-infectious because the recipient belongs to the protected sub-cohort.

The time-declining expression

h_v(t)= λ(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}]

that is repeatedly quoted for the overestimate claim is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected at time t, i.e. the hazard in the still-at-risk risk set. It falls because the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort is progressively depleted by infection while the p never-at-risk fraction continues to accrue event-free person-time. That is a selection/depletion artefact of conditioning on survival, not the marginal incidence rate that an IRR estimates.

Counting person-time contributed by the permanently immune with zero events is not denominator inflation. Protected subjects are still having exposure opportunities; they simply have zero events on that time. Their zero-risk person-time is exactly how a population average rate expresses a reduction in risk per exposure. Removing it would condition on susceptibility and change the estimand to the hazard among residual susceptibles, which is not the per-exposure efficacy the rate ratio is designed for.

On the same mixture

S_V(t)=p+(1-p)S_U(t) ⇒ F_V(t)=(1-p)F_U(t) ⇒ RR(t)=1-p

so 1-RR = p = 1-IRR on the population average scale. The apparent time dependence of the A derivations is the conditional-on-survival hazard among survivors, and the fact that their time-averaged IRR(T)→0 as T→∞ is the tell: the vaccine does not become perfect with longer follow-up. The marginal, population-average reduction per exposure opportunity is p, and the incidence rate ratio recovers that susceptibility efficacy without systematic bias.

I’m staying with C. The disagreement is really about what we mean by “per-exposure” and whether we are talking about a marginal population rate or a conditional hazard among survivors.

On the epidemiologic scale the incidence rate is events per total person-time at risk, i.e. the marginal population average hazard over the whole vaccinated cohort. For an all-or-nothing mechanism that is a simple mixture.

Let λ0 be the unvaccinated per-exposure hazard. A fraction p is rendered completely non-susceptible, hazard 0 per exposure, and a fraction 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated, hazard λ0. The marginal hazard that events/total person-time estimates is

h_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0,
h_U = λ0

so

IRR = h_V / h_U = 1-p,    1-IRR = p

constant in time and independent of follow-up length. That p is the population-average reduction in risk per unit exposure time, i.e. per exposure opportunity experienced by the vaccinated cohort: the proportion of exposures rendered non-infectious because the recipient is in the protected sub-cohort. The p fraction still accrues exposure time; they simply have zero events on that time. Counting that zero-event person-time is exactly how a population average rate is defined. Removing it would re-define the estimand to “hazard among the residual susceptibles”, a conditional within-stratum quantity, not the marginal per-exposure effect an IRR is built to capture.

The time-decreasing expression

h_V(t)= λ(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}]

that is quoted for the overestimate position is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected up to t, i.e. the hazard in the still-at-risk risk set. It declines because the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort is progressively depleted by infection while the p never-at-risk fraction continues to accrue event-free person-time. That is a selection/depletion artefact of conditioning on survival, not a change in the per-exposure risk for an individual who remains susceptible. A susceptible vaccinee continues to have per-exposure risk λ0; the conditional hazard is falling because the composition of the still-uninfected group changes.

On the standard marginal definition the cumulative risk ratio agrees:

S_V(t)=p+(1-p)S_U(t)  ⇒  F_V(t)=(1-p)F_U(t)  ⇒  RR(t)=1-p,

so 1-RR = p = 1-IRR on the population average scale. The apparent time dependence of IRR(T) = (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]/[pλT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] is the time-averaged conditional hazard among survivors, not the marginal incidence density that is routinely estimated from events / total person-time. 

If “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” is taken in its usual epidemiologic sense – the average reduction in infection probability per exposure opportunity at the cohort level, i.e. susceptibility efficacy – the rate ratio recovers the proportion protected p without systematic bias. The instantaneous HR(0)=1-p is a within-entry theoretical construct conditional on being susceptible at time zero; the quantity an IRR is designed to estimate in practice is the marginal population average per exposure, which is p.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The all-or-nothing model with proportion p completely protected and 1-p fully susceptible with baseline hazard λ gives

S_u = exp(-λt), S_v = p + (1-p)exp(-λt)
h_u = λ
h_v(t)= λ(1-p)exp(-λt)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λt)]
HR(t)= (1-p)exp(-λt)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λt)], HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)↓0.

Instantaneous per-exposure reduction at entry is 1-HR(0)=p. Cumulative risk ratio is constant
RR(t)=[1-S_v]/[1-S_u]=1-p so 1-RR=p is the proportion protected.

With the conventional events/total person-time incidence density to T
IR_u = λ
IR_v(T)= (1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pT+(1-p)(1-exp(-λT))/λ]
IRR(T)= IR_v/IR_u = (1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pλT+(1-p)(1-exp(-λT))] <1-p
for T>0, IRR(0)=1-p, IRR→0 as T→∞.
Hence 1-IRR(T) > p, bias increasing with follow-up and 1-IRR→1. The time-averaged HR is below HR(0) because the p protected fraction keeps contributing event-free person-time while the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted by infection.

This is classic all-or-nothing vs leaky: risk ratio constant =1-p for all-or-nothing, rate ratio constant for leaky. The incidence density ratio is a time-averaged hazard ratio that is diluted by never-at-risk person-time, so 1-IRR is upwardly biased for the instantaneous/per-exposure reduction p and for the proportion protected. Overestimation increases with follow-up, equality only as T→0.

- C correctly estimate camp 2,5,7,13,14,16,17,21: treat marginal hazard as mixture h_V = p·0+(1-p)λ constant, so IRR=1-p and 1-IRR=p = population-average per-exposure reduction. On marginal population-average definition per-exposure VE = proportion protected.
- B underestimate camp essentially absent in round 3.

Current best synthesis retains standard survival derivation with usual total person-time denominator: incidence density ratio declines with follow-up, 1-IRR > p, i.e. overestimates the instantaneous per-exposure/proportion-protected efficacy, with equality only as T→0. Risk ratio 1-RR=p is the unbiased all-or-nothing estimator. Minority C interpretation hinges on redefining per-exposure VE as marginal mixture hazard and conflating marginal mixture with conditional hazard used in IRR calculations. Unresolved wording remains about whether “per-exposure” is intended as instantaneous biological reduction in the susceptible stratum, HR(0)=1-p, versus population-average reduction per exposure opportunity, p.

The all-or-nothing model with proportion p completely protected and 1-p fully susceptible with baseline hazard λ gives

S_u = exp(-λt), S_v = p + (1-p)exp(-λt)
h_u = λ
h_v(t)= λ(1-p)exp(-λt)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λt)]
HR(t)= (1-p)exp(-λt)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λt)], HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)↓0.

Instantaneous per-exposure reduction at entry is 1-HR(0)=p. Cumulative risk ratio is constant
RR(t)=[1-S_v]/[1-S_u]=1-p so 1-RR=p is the proportion protected.

With the conventional events/total person-time incidence density to T
IR_u = λ

for T>0, IRR(0)=1-p, IRR→0 as T→∞.

S0=exp(-λt), Sv=p+(1-p)S0,
hv(t)=λ(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0], h0=λ,
HR(t)=hv/h0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0], HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)↓0 monotone.
Cumulative risk ratio RR(t)=[1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p, so 1-RR=p constant = proportion protected.

On total person-time denominator
IRu=λ,
IRv(T)=(1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pT+(1-p)(1-exp(-λT))/λ],
IRR(T)=(1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pλT+(1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]]<1-p ∀T>0,
lim T→0 IRR=1-p, lim T→∞ IRR=0.
Hence 1-IRR(T)>p with bias growing with follow-up →1. This is the time-averaged hazard ratio < HR(0) because the p protected fraction keeps contributing event-free person-time while the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted.

A camp – 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 in round 3 – treats per-exposure VE as instantaneous/biological reduction for an individual who remains at risk, VEpe=1-HR(0)=p, i.e. the proportion protected and the constant risk ratio 1-RR=p. Classic all-or-nothing vs leaky: RR constant for all-or-nothing, IRR constant for leaky.

Marginal mixture hazard = p·0+(1-p)λ=(1-p)λ, so IRR =1-p, 1-IRR=p constant in time. The hv(t) decreasing expression is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected, a selection/depletion artefact of conditioning on survival. Protected person-time with zero events is legitimate denominator for a marginal rate; counting it scales the population rate down by 1-p. On this marginal definition RR=1-p and IRR=1-p coincide, so 1-IRR recovers susceptibility efficacy without bias.

Hence 1-IRR(T)=1-(1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pλT+(1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]] >p, increasing with follow-up →1.

So time-averaged rate ratio is below initial hazard ratio because p protected keep contributing event-free person-time while 1-p susceptible are depleted. Conventional 1-incidence rate ratio therefore overstates the instantaneous per-exposure reduction 1-HR(0)=p and the constant risk ratio 1-RR=p. Bias grows with follow-up, disappears only T→0. Cumulative risk ratio is constant RR(t)=1-p so 1-RR=p proportion protected. On total person-time to T, IRR(T)=(1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pλT+(1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]] <1-p for T>0, →1-p as T→0, →0 as T→∞. Hence 1-IRR(T)>p, increasing with follow-up to 1.

A-overestimate camp in round 3: conventional events/total-person-time IRR is time-averaged HR. The p completely protected contribute event-free person-time while the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted by infection, so the marginal time-averaged HR < HR(0)=1-p and 1-IRR(T)>1-HR(0)=p=1-RR. Instantaneous per-exposure / proportion-protected VE is VEpe(0)=1-HR(0)=p, risk ratio is constant 1-p, rate ratio is the appropriate leaky estimator. Equality only in T→0 rare-disease limit. Classic all-or-nothing vs leaky swap.

C-correctly-estimate camp in round 3: IRR estimates the marginal population-average rate. Biology is a mixture: h_V = p·0+(1-p)λ = (1-p)λ, h_U=λ, so IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p constant. Protected person-time with zero events is legitimate exposure time with zero risk; counting it gives the population-average reduction per exposure opportunity, i.e. susceptibility efficacy. The time-decreasing h_v(t)=λ(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}] is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected, i.e. conditional on the still-at-risk set, which declines by selection/depletion of the 1-p susceptibles. The apparent IRR(T)<1-p is the time average of that conditional hazard, not the marginal incidence density routinely reported. On the marginal scale S_v=p+(1-p)S_u ⇒ F_v=(1-p)F_u ⇒ RR=1-p =1-IRR.

Disagreement is definitional: instantaneous hazard reduction in the susceptible stratum / proportion protected p versus population-average reduction per exposure opportunity p. Under the standard textbook instantaneous per-exposure / proportion-protected definition 1-IRR overstates VE for finite follow-up; under a marginal mixture / population-average definition 1-IRR = p exactly.

Current lean remains A overestimate for the usual epidemiologic phrasing that the conventional 1-incidence rate ratio overestimates the biological per-exposure/proportion-protected efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine, with the noted C nuance about marginal vs conditional hazard and the exact wording of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” remaining unresolved.
reflection_text.10:
The mathematics is stable across rounds and consistent in the A camp.

All-or-nothing with fraction p completely protected, 1-p fully susceptible, unvaccinated constant hazard λ:
S_u = exp(-λt), S_v = p + (1-p)exp(-λt)
h_u = λ
h_v(t)= λ(1-p)exp(-λt)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λt)]
HR(t)=h_v/h_u = (1-p)exp(-λt)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λt)], HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)↓0
True instantaneous per-exposure reduction at entry =1-HR(0)=p, proportion protected.
Cumulative risk ratio constant: RR(t)=[1-S_v]/[1-S_u]=1-p so 1-RR=p.

Person-time incidence rate up to T with total person-time denominator:
IR_u = λ
IR_v(T) = (1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pT+(1-p)(1-exp(-λT))/λ]
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pλT+(1-p)(1-exp(-λT))] <1-p for T>0
lim T→0 IRR=1-p, lim T→∞ IRR=0
Hence 1-IRR(T)>p for any T>0, increasing with follow-up →1.

Classic all-or-nothing vs leaky: risk ratio constant for all-or-nothing, rate ratio declines with time; for leaky hazard ratio constant and 1-IRR estimates per-exposure VE correctly.

Round 3 public split persists:
A overestimate: 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8. Argument: 1-IRR is a time-averaged HR <HR(0). Protected p fraction continues to contribute event-free person-time while 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted, so marginal time-averaged HR falls below initial HR(0)=1-p, hence 1-IRR>p=1-HR(0)=1-RR. Unbiased all-or-nothing estimator on cumulative scale is 1-RR=p; rate ratio overstates instantaneous per-exposure reduction, overstatement grows with T, vanishes only as T→0.

C correctly estimate: 13,14,16,17,2,5,7,21,9. Argument: per-exposure VE is population-average reduction per exposure. Marginal hazard =p·0+(1-p)λ=(1-p)λ constant, so IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p. The declining h_v(t) is hazard conditional on remaining uninfected, a selection/depletion artefact. Protected person-time with zero events is legitimate denominator for a population rate; counting it is not denominator inflation. On this marginal definition both RR and IRR recover p.

Unresolved definitional nuance remains:
* instantaneous hazard reduction for whole cohort / proportion protected p=1-HR(0). Under conventional teaching 1-IRR overestimates p with finite follow-up, unbiased only at T→0.
* population-average susceptibility effect =p. Under this definition marginal rate ratio is constant and unbiased, and the time-declining conditional hazard is a re-expression of depletion.

Current leaning stays with conventional epidemiologic teaching A overestimate: on the usual total-person-time incidence density definition 1-IRR is time-averaged and >p, with risk ratio 1-RR=p being the unbiased all-or-nothing estimator. The C camp’s constant marginal hazard argument holds only if per-exposure efficacy is re-defined as the population-average susceptibility effect and the conditional-on-survival hazard is treated as artefact.

Key points to retain: formulas for S_v, h_v(t), HR(t), RR(t), IRR(T); limiting behaviour; long-term bias 1-IRR→1; short-time limit recovers p; leaky vs all-or-nothing swap. No new mathematical corrections emerged in round 3.
reflection_text.12:
Mechanistic core is settled and stable across rounds.

All-or-nothing with proportion p completely immune, 1-p fully susceptible with hazard λ.

S_u = exp(-λt); S_v = p + (1-p)S_u
h_u = λ
h_v(t)= λ(1-p)S_u /[p+(1-p)S_u]
HR(t)= (1-p)S_u/[p+(1-p)S_u] , HR(0)=1-p monotone ↓ to 0.

Cumulative risk ratio RR(t)=[1-S_v]/[1-S_u]=1-p constant, 1-RR=p = proportion protected.

Total person-time incidence rate to T:
IR_u = λ
IR_v(T)= (1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pT+(1-p)λ^{-1}[1-exp(-λT)]]
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]/[pλT+(1-p)[1-exp(-λT)]] <1-p ∀T>0
lim T→0 IRR=1-p , lim T→∞ IRR=0
Hence 1-IRR(T) > p with bias growing with follow-up →1.

That is the A overestimate derivation reiterated in round 3 by 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8. It treats per-exposure VE as instantaneous hazard reduction at entry, VE_pe=1-HR(0)=p, and notes observed IRR is a time-averaged hazard ratio diluted by pT event-free person-time and depletion of the 1-p susceptible subcohort. Risk ratio is the constant all-or-nothing estimator; rate ratio is the leaky estimator.

C correctly estimate camp 13,14,16,17,2,5,7,21,9 argues marginal population hazard is constant: h_v^pop = p·0+(1-p)λ = (1-p)λ, so IRR_pop =1-p and 1-IRR=p is the population-average reduction per exposure / proportion protected. The decreasing h_v(t) above is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected, i.e. conditional on survival/selection in the shrinking risk set. On the marginal rate scale protected subjects legitimately contribute person-time with zero events, which is how the average rate scales by 1-p. Under this definition the rate ratio recovers the susceptibility efficacy without bias and is symmetric to the leaky-risk distinction.

B underestimate arguments are essentially gone.

Unresolved is definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy”. If defined as instantaneous biological reduction per exposure for the whole cohort / at entry, conventional total-person-time 1-IRR >p, i.e. overestimates the proportion protected/instantaneous HR(0). If defined as population-average marginal reduction in risk per exposure opportunity, 1-IRR =p is unbiased. Majority detailed derivations keep the classic all-or-nothing vs leaky distinction: 1-RR constant, 1-IRR time-dependent and upwardly biased for p. That is the synthesis I am keeping as best current; the C position is a re-definition of the estimand to the marginal mixture hazard.

Vaccinated mixture: Sv(t)=p+(1-p)exp(-λt)
hv(t)= -Sv′/Sv = λ(1-p)exp(-λt)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λt)]
HR(t)=hv/h0 = (1-p)exp(-λt)/[p+(1-p)exp(-λt)], HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)↓0.

RR(t)=[1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p, 1-RR=p = proportion protected.

Person-time averaged incidence rate to T with total person-time denominator:
IR0=λ

lim T→0 IRR=1-p, lim T→∞ IRR=0.
Hence 1-IRR(T) > p =1-RR, bias ↑ with follow-up, →1.

So on the usual total person-time definition the time-averaged rate ratio is < the initial hazard ratio and 1-IRR is upwardly biased for the instantaneous per-exposure reduction p. The risk ratio 1-RR=p is the unbiased all-or-nothing estimator; for a leaky vaccine the converse holds.

Disagreement in the room is definitional/selection.

A camp, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,3,4,6,8,20, says:
1-IRR overestimates the instantaneous biological per-exposure reduction p because protected p fraction keeps contributing event-free person-time while the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted. C camp, colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,7,9,21 says:
Per-exposure VE is the population-average reduction in risk per exposure opportunity. Marginal population hazard = p·0+(1-p)λ = (1-p)λ constant. IRR =1-p, 1-IRR=p. The unresolved nuance remains: does “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” mean
1) instantaneous hazard reduction for a susceptible individual, VE_pe=1-HR(0)=p, or zero conditional on the susceptible subcohort, or
2) population-average reduction in risk per exposure, i.e. the proportion protected p.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

The algebra on both sides is correct, the disagreement is about which quantity an incidence rate ratio is actually estimating in a cohort study.

In practice an incidence rate is events divided by total person-time of exposure accumulated by the cohort. That is a marginal population-average hazard. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the vaccinated cohort is a mixture: fraction p has per-exposure hazard 0, fraction 1-p has the unvaccinated per-exposure hazard λ0. Marginally

h_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0
h_U = λ0

so the rate ratio that a study reports is

IRR = h_V / h_U = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

constant in time and independent of follow-up. That p is the average reduction in risk per unit exposure time, per exposure opportunity experienced by the vaccinated cohort, i.e. the proportion of exposures rendered non-infectious because the recipient belongs to the protected sub-cohort. Protected individuals are still accumulating exposure time; they simply have zero events on that time. Counting that zero-event person-time is how a population average rate is defined, it is not denominator inflation.

The expressions

h_v(t)= λ(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}], HR(t)=(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}]

used to argue for overestimation are the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected up to t, i.e. the hazard in the still-at-risk set. It declines because the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort is progressively depleted by infection while the p never-at-risk fraction continues to accrue event-free person-time. That is a selection/depletion artefact of conditioning on survival, not the marginal incidence density that an IRR estimates.

On the marginal scale the risk ratio agrees: S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_u(t) ⇒ F_v(t)=(1-p)F_u(t) ⇒ RR(t)=1-p, so 1-RR = p = 1-IRR on the population-average scale. The apparent time dependence of the time-averaged IRR(T) = (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]/[pλT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] is the average of the conditional hazard HR(t) over follow-up. It tends to 1-p in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit and it is not the estimand the conventional events/person-time ratio targets.

If per-exposure vaccine efficacy is taken in its usual epidemiologic operational sense – the average reduction in infection probability per exposure opportunity at the cohort level, the susceptibility efficacy – the incidence rate ratio recovers the proportion protected p without systematic bias for an all-or-nothing mechanism. Redefining the target to the instantaneous hazard at entry HR(0)=1-p conditional on still being susceptible changes the estimand to a within-susceptible conditional hazard, not the marginal per-exposure effect an IRR is built to capture in field studies.

C. correctly estimate

The algebra on both sides is correct, the disagreement is about which quantity an incidence rate ratio is actually estimating in a cohort study.

In practice an incidence rate is events divided by total person-time of exposure accumulated by the cohort. That is a marginal population-average hazard. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the vaccinated cohort is a mixture: fraction p has per-exposure hazard 0, fraction 1-p has the unvaccinated per-exposure hazard λ0. Marginally

h_V = p·0 + (1-p)·λ0 = (1-p) λ0
h_U = λ0

so the rate ratio that a study reports is

IRR = h_V / h_U = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

constant in time and independent of follow-up. That p is the average reduction in risk per unit exposure time, per exposure opportunity experienced by the vaccinated cohort, i.e. the proportion of exposures rendered non-infectious because the recipient belongs to the protected sub-cohort. Protected individuals are still accumulating exposure time; they simply have zero events on that time. Counting that zero-event person-time is how a population average rate is defined, it is not denominator inflation.

The expressions

h_v(t)= λ(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}], HR(t)=(1-p)e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}]

used to argue for overestimation are the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected up to t, i.e. the hazard in the still-at-risk set. It declines because the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort is progressively depleted by infection while the p never-at-risk fraction continues to accrue event-free person-time. That is a selection/depletion artefact of conditioning on survival, not the marginal incidence density that an IRR estimates.

On the marginal scale the risk ratio agrees: S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_u(t) ⇒ F_v(t)=(1-p)F_u(t) ⇒ RR(t)=1-p, so 1-RR = p = 1-IRR on the population-average scale. The apparent time dependence of the time-averaged IRR(T) = (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]/[pλT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] is the average of the conditional hazard HR(t) over follow-up. It tends to 1-p in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit and it is not the estimand the conventional events/person-time ratio targets.

If per-exposure vaccine efficacy is taken in its usual epidemiologic operational sense – the average reduction in infection probability per exposure opportunity at the cohort level, the susceptibility efficacy – the incidence rate ratio recovers the proportion protected p without systematic bias for an all-or-nothing mechanism. Redefining the target to the instantaneous hazard at entry HR(0)=1-p conditional on still being susceptible changes the estimand to a within-susceptible conditional hazard, not the marginal per-exposure effect an IRR is built to capture in field studies.

* Monotone decreasing HR(t) is a conditional-on-survival artefact, not a change in marginal per-exposure risk.

* Instantaneous VEpe=1-HR(0)=p vs time-averaged 1-IRR.
* Risk ratio constant, rate ratio declines for all-or-nothing; reverse for leaky.
